# Chapter 3: Your First Hive

When I bought my first colony, I was told two things by two different people. The first said, "Leave them alone and they will do fine." The second said, "Check them every week or you will lose them." Both were right, and that tension is the subject of this chapter.

## What arrives in the box

A package of bees weighs about three pounds and holds roughly ten thousand workers and a caged queen. The cage is a small wooden box with a screen, about the size of a matchbox, and in it sits a queen who has never seen your hive. Do not be alarmed by the sound. A package is loud, and it smells sweet.

Your first job is to get everyone into the hive without crushing anyone. Choose a calm afternoon with temperatures above fifty degrees. Wear a veil and gloves if you want them; I did, for the first two years, and then found that I moved more slowly with gloves and was stung more, not less.

1. Spray the bees lightly with sugar water. A bee that is licking itself is not thinking about you.
2. Remove the queen cage and check that she is alive. She should be moving.
3. Hang the cage between two frames, candy end up.
4. Tap the package sharply on the ground to drop the bees to the bottom, then pour them over the frames in a single, confident motion.

## The first week

Resist the urge to open the hive. Every inspection costs the colony a day of work. In the first week, the bees are chewing through the candy plug to release the queen, and you should leave them alone to do it. Fill the feeder with one-to-one sugar syrup and check it from the outside.

On day seven, open the hive on a warm afternoon. You are looking for three things: the queen released and gone from the cage, fresh wax on the foundation, and eggs, small grains of rice standing upright in the bottom of the cells. If you see eggs, you have a queen. If you do not, do not panic; look again tomorrow with better light.

## A note on being stung

You will be stung. It is not the end of the hobby. Keep your movements slow and your breathing even, and remember that the bees are far more interested in the work in front of them than in you. In my first season I was stung eleven times; in my fifth, twice.

## Weeks two to six: building up

By the second week the colony will be drawing out comb on its own, and the feeder will need refilling every few days. The question every new keeper asks is how often to look inside. My rule is every ten days until the first brood box is nine-tenths full, and then every two weeks. Each visit has the same four questions:

- Is there a queen? (Eggs, or very young larvae, are enough to tell you.)
- Is there room? A colony that runs out of space in May will swarm in June.
- Is the brood pattern solid, or spotty? A patchy pattern may mean a failing queen, disease or just a cold spell.
- Are there signs of trouble: chalky mummies, sunken cappings, a sour smell, small beetles running across the frames?

Write the answers down. I carry a pencil and a small notebook in my back pocket, and after twenty minutes with a hive I cannot reliably remember what I saw. The notebook is more valuable than any piece of equipment I own.

### When to add the second box

When seven of the ten frames in the lower box are covered with bees and at least six hold comb, add the second box. Do not wait for the bees to be crowded. Add it a week before you think you need to, because a colony that feels cramped is a colony that begins planning to leave.

### What went wrong in my first hive

I lost my first colony in the second November, and I want to describe how, because the mistakes are common ones. I did not treat for mites in August because the hive looked strong. I did not weigh the hive before winter, so I did not know how little honey was in it. And I took off the entrance reducer too early, which let mice in. Any one of these I might have survived. All three together were more than the bees could handle.

The consolation is that each of those mistakes has a simple remedy, and the rest of this book is about them. In the next chapter we will talk about the mite, which is the single largest reason beginners lose their first colony, and how to count them with a jar of powdered sugar.
